q: What is analysis in business analysis?
options: Examining, breaking down and clarifying information to understand, complete and improve it
explanation: Analysis is the process of examining, breaking down, synthesizing and clarifying information to further understand it, complete it and improve it. Drawing information out is elicitation.

q: Into which five categories does PMI's guide organize analysis models?
explanation: The models are organized into five categories: scope models (bounding the solution), process models (how it will be used), rule models (rules to enforce), data models (data and its life cycle) and interface models (how it interacts with systems and users).

q: An analyst must agree with stakeholders what is inside and outside a new booking solution. She draws the solution in the middle, with every system and person that exchanges something with it. Which model is this?
explanation: A context diagram is a scope model that shows all the direct system and human interfaces to systems within a solution, with the inputs and outputs between them. It is created early to define scope.

q: An analyst must make sure no combination of loan-approval conditions has been overlooked. Which model is best?
explanation: Decision tables are useful for ensuring that the analyst has considered all possible combinations of decision scenarios and related outcomes. A decision tree shows the flow and order of decisions.

q: Which model shows the valid conditions an order can be in (placed, paid, shipped, delivered) and the allowed moves between them?
explanation: The state table and state diagram are data models that show the valid states of an object and any allowed transitions between those states.

q: A team is unsure whether one customer can hold several accounts, and whether an account can belong to two customers. Which model shows these data objects and how many of each relate to the other?
explanation: An entity relationship diagram is a data model showing the business data objects of interest and the cardinality relationship between them: how many times one entity occurs in relation to another.

q: What is a use case?
options: A one-sentence requirement from the user's point of view
A text narrative of the interactions between a user and the system to achieve a goal, with normal, alternative and exception flows
A static picture of one screen
explanation: A use case is a process model that uses textual narrative to describe the system-user interactions needed to complete a goal. It contains a normal flow plus alternative and exception flows.

q: A complex interaction with many exception paths must be fully specified for an external contractor. Which form of requirement fits best?
explanation: Use cases describe complex interactions between users and systems in detail, including alternative and exception flows. A user story is deliberately brief and relies on conversation for its detail.

q: What does the acronym DEEP describe?
options: A well-refined product backlog: detailed appropriately, estimated, emergent, prioritized
The stages of an elicitation activity
explanation: DEEP describes the characteristics of a well-refined product backlog: detailed appropriately, estimated, emergent and prioritized. INVEST describes a good user story.

q: A user story is too large to build in one iteration. What should the team do?
options: Assign more developers to it so it fits in one iteration
Slice it into smaller stories that each deliver value
explanation: Story slicing splits epics or user stories into smaller increments of value that can be built within one iteration. Large stories are commonly called epics.

q: Stakeholders have confirmed the notes from three workshops. A developer says: "Good, those are the requirements now, so we can start building." Are confirmed elicitation results the same as requirements?
options: Yes, once confirmed they are final requirements
No. They still need analysis to avoid missing, inconsistent or conflicting requirements
Yes, if the sponsor attended the session
No, they are discarded after the session
explanation: Even though elicitation results come from knowledgeable stakeholders, they are not the final requirements without additional analysis. They are used with the analysis models so the whole solution is analyzed.

q: What are acceptance criteria?
options: Concrete and demonstrable conditions that must be met for the business to accept an item
The list of stakeholders who must sign the charter
explanation: Acceptance criteria are concrete and demonstrable conditions about an item that must be met for the business stakeholders or customers to accept it. They form the basis of acceptance tests.

q: "Given I am signed in, when I select 'export', then a spreadsheet is downloaded." What is this?
options: A transition requirement for moving to the future state
An acceptance criterion in the given-when-then format
explanation: Behavior-driven development uses the given-when-then format for acceptance criteria: given the preconditions, when the user does something, then the product reacts in a stated way.

q: How do the definition of ready and the definition of done differ?
options: Ready: conditions before work on a story begins. Done: conditions before an item is considered complete and acceptable.
Ready applies to the project; done applies to the portfolio
Ready is set by the sponsor; done by the vendor
explanation: The definition of ready is a series of conditions the team agrees a story must meet before work begins. The definition of done is a series of conditions an item must meet before it is considered sufficiently developed to be accepted.

q: What does Verify Requirements check?
options: That the requirements meet the business goals and stakeholder needs
That the requirements are of sufficient quality and meet standards
That the solution has been released
explanation: Verify Requirements checks that requirements are of sufficient quality: free of errors and conflicts and compliant with standards. Checking that they meet business goals and objectives is validation.

q: A requirement is clearly written and meets every standard, but no stakeholder actually needs it. Which check would catch this?
explanation: Validation checks that requirements meet the business goals and objectives and stakeholder needs. Verified requirements are not a guarantee that they address the business need.

q: A safety-critical requirements document is reviewed by a trained team that follows a checklist and records every defect it finds. Which type of peer review is this, the most formal one?
explanation: From least to most formal, the peer reviews are the peer desk check, the walkthrough and the inspection. An inspection is a formal, rigorous review for completeness, consistency and conformance to standards, often with a checklist.

q: Which technique is the main verification check for user stories on adaptive projects?
explanation: INVEST (independent, negotiable, valuable, estimable, small, testable) describes the characteristics a user story needs to be good and ready for development. It is the primary verification technique in adaptive approaches.

q: During validation, what must every requirement trace back to?
options: The project schedule and its milestones
explanation: Validation ensures that all requirements trace back to the business goals and objectives, so that what is to be built will actually meet them.

q: What is the business analyst's role in prioritizing requirements?
options: To facilitate and negotiate, while accountable stakeholders make the decisions
To leave prioritization entirely to the developers, who know the effort best of all
explanation: A business analyst may recommend priorities, but accountable stakeholders with the authority to prioritize must be involved. The analyst facilitates and negotiates prioritization decisions.

q: Which two kinds of information are combined when prioritizing a requirement?
options: Its section number in the document and its current approval status
Its business value, and the team's estimate of effort and risk
explanation: Prioritization commonly involves two efforts: business stakeholders or product owners prioritize by estimated business value, and the project team provides estimates of effort and risk.

q: What often results from a product risk response?
explanation: Product risk responses may include modifying or adding product requirements or project activities. Product risk management therefore helps find and resolve gaps in the requirements.

q: How does product design differ from requirements?
options: Design states why the project exists
Requirements say what the product should do; design is about how it is built or looks
Design is done before the business case
explanation: Assessing product design goes beyond what the product should do and focuses on how it should be built or how it should look. Business analysis evaluates the design options and recommends among them.

q: On an adaptive project, a stakeholder writes a new user story and asks the scrum master to put it at the top of the backlog. Who decides whether and where it goes?
explanation: Although anyone can write a user story, the product owner decides whether and where to place the story in the backlog.

q: Stakeholders have approved the wording of a requirement, but the testers say they cannot tell when it would be satisfied. What is missing?
options: A full business case for the requirement
A persona for the requirement's users
A situation statement for the need
explanation: Acceptance criteria are the concrete and demonstrable conditions that must be met for an item to be accepted. They form the basis of acceptance tests and help show where a requirement is unclear.

q: A team is about to start building a user story that has no acceptance criteria yet. The product owner says they can be added after the work is done. What does Business Analysis for Practitioners say?
options: That is fine, as long as the story is small
At least one criterion should be written before work begins
Acceptance criteria are needed only for defects found in testing
The testers alone should write them afterwards
explanation: Before work can begin on a deliverable or user story, the practitioner should ensure that at least one acceptance criterion is written, so the team knows exactly what is required.

q: A user story has grown to seven acceptance criteria. According to Business Analysis for Practitioners, what should the team consider?
options: Dividing the story into two or more stories
Deleting criteria until only one remains
Moving the criteria into the definition of done
Asking the sponsor to approve each criterion
explanation: If a deliverable or user story has more than three acceptance criteria, it may be good to divide it into two or more, to help the team implement the feature quickly and efficiently.

q: A team's checklist says every increment must have passed regression testing and security validation, and have its documentation complete. A developer calls these "the acceptance criteria". Which term is correct?
options: Acceptance criteria, since they are tested
Business rules, since they constrain the team
The definition of ready, since they must be met before any work starts
The definition of done, since they apply to the whole increment
explanation: The definition of done applies to the entire product increment: documentation, regression testing, security validation, production support readiness. Acceptance criteria are specific to one deliverable, user story or feature.

q: "Recipe emails are sent only to customers who have opted in." This statement holds whichever mailing system the company uses. What kind of statement is it?
explanation: Business rules describe policies, standards or regulations that constrain how the business operates. They are system-agnostic: they define how the business operates regardless of systems and technology.

q: In a workshop, stakeholders place sticky notes on a drawing: infrastructure at the roots, main functions on the branches, new features as leaves. Features far from the trunk may be cut off. Which tool is this, and where do the top priorities go?
options: A fishbone diagram, with priorities at the head
A product tree, with priorities nearest the trunk
A story map, with priorities on the right
An onion diagram, with priorities in the outer layer
explanation: On a product tree the roots and trunk are the infrastructure, the branches the primary functions and the leaves new features. The highest-priority items are placed near the bottom, closest to the trunk; items farther out come later or are pruned.

q: During MoSCoW prioritization, a feature is marked "won't have". The developers are unsure whether to keep its design in mind. What does Business Analysis for Practitioners say the team should make clear?
options: Whether "won't" means not at this time or not at any point
Whether the feature was proposed by the sponsor
Whether the feature should be marked "must" instead
Whether all of the stakeholders voted on it unanimously at the workshop
explanation: Defining the "won't have" items is important so the team understands whether it means won't have at any point or won't have at this time.

q: An analyst sketches each screen of a planned booking application with boxes and labels: a rectangle where the logo will be, lines for the input fields. No colors or real images. What is this, and what is it for?
options: A high-fidelity prototype, to demonstrate the finished design to customers
A data model, to show how bookings are stored
A wireframe, to align the team and stakeholders on the requirements
A use case, to describe the steps of making a booking
explanation: A wireframe is a low-fidelity drawing of the proposed application showing the key elements of the user interface and their layout. It is kept simple and used to make sure the team and business stakeholders are aligned on the requirements.
